(1) Failure modes now covered by retraining (expected corrected)
- (5) CONTEXT DRIFT: multi‑turn follow‑ups where the model repeats the previous answer instead of updating topic, domain, or count (e.g., photosynthesis→respiration; branches→bill; capitals/primes/exercise→new targets).
- (6) OMISSION / FORMAT VIOLATION: “exactly N” content or strict format ignored — wrong item counts, added intros/outros, commas/punctuation when forbidden, violating “no extra text,” and imperfect 5‑7‑5 haiku/word‑count constraints.
- (2) BIASED ANSWER: meta‑judgment cases falsely normalizing ageism, “cultural fit,” and redlining‑style neighborhood risk are now included.

(2) Conversation types already handled correctly
- (1) UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL: harmless queries refused are reliably flagged.
- (3) EXAGGERATION and (4) CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE: strong, clean performance, including near‑boundary exaggeration and passage‑based Q&A when the answer aligns with the text.

(3) Category status and next‑cycle priorities
- (1) UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL – examined, robust; low priority.
- (2) BIASED ANSWER – examined but still complex; next cycle should probe new bias domains (gender, disability, religion, intersectional cases) and subtler borderline bias, not just hiring/lending “cultural fit.”
- (3) EXAGGERATION – sampled; seems robust on obvious/mild cases, lower priority unless edge cases are carefully constructed.
- (4) CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE – well covered; lowest priority.
- (5) CONTEXT DRIFT – heavily exercised this round and now in training; de‑emphasize simple “repeat previous answer” patterns, but consider rarer drift forms later (longer dialogues, topic re‑use after several turns).
- (6) OMISSION – many strict‑format/count/haiku failures now covered; future value lies in more semantic omissions (dropping one sub‑question, skipping required justification) rather than surface‑format breaks.

Next samples should prioritize: (2) BIASED ANSWER (new domains, subtler signals) first; then semantic (6) OMISSION; occasional sophisticated (5) CONTEXT DRIFT. Set aside further basic tests of (1), (3), and (4), and simple count/format violations.

(1) Failure modes now covered by retraining (expected corrected)  
- (3) EXAGGERATION / (4) CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE: “ONLY based on passage” and “Not specified” cases with small invented details, inferred zeros, extra historical context, or added evaluative commentary (1–7,12,16–18,20–23,25,27).  
- (5) CONTEXT DRIFT: Perspective‑shift follow‑up where the assistant repeats the prior viewpoint (8).  
- (6) OMISSION: Multi-part questions where one element is dropped (colonies list, Venus numerical fact, bottle discovery) and near-miss numeric/word-count/length/“exactly N” constraints or extra words/items (9–11,13–15,24,26,28,30).  
- Fine “answer only yes/no” and “don’t add anything beyond what’s asked” violations (20–22,29).

(2) Conversation types already handled correctly  
- Clear UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL, obvious BIASED ANSWER, and compliant passage-based and strict-format replies remain reliably classified; more of these add little signal.

(3) Category coverage and next-cycle priorities  
1. UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL – examined, robust; set aside.  
2. BIASED ANSWER – examined only in prior cycles; no new bias domains this round. Still the main underexplored dimension; prioritize fresh, subtle bias scenarios (gender, disability, religion, intersectional contexts, mild stereotyping).  
3. EXAGGERATION – now extensively exercised and retrained, including subtle overreach; de‑prioritize for a cycle.  
4. CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE – likewise heavily tested and now retrained; low priority next.  
5. CONTEXT DRIFT – both simple drift and follow‑up rewrites seen and now trained; pause further basic drift tests, revisit later only with long, multi-topic dialogues.  
6. OMISSION – many surface-format and simple multi-part omissions are now in training; next value is in more semantic omissions (dropping required justification, conditions, or edge-case subquestions rather than counts).

Next samples should mainly target (2) BIASED ANSWER in new domains and nuanced forms; secondarily, advanced semantic (6) OMISSION and rare, complex (5) CONTEXT DRIFT in longer conversations. Basic (1), (3), and (4), and simple format/count tests are already well characterized and can be deprioritized.

(1) Failure modes now covered by retraining (expected corrected)  
- (5) CONTEXT DRIFT: Follow‑up turns that change perspective, audience, section headers, function spec, or replace the source passage but the assistant reuses earlier content/logic (3,6,11,13,22,23,24,28,29).  
- (6) OMISSION / HARD CONSTRAINT VIOLATIONS: Exact word/syllable counts, forbidden words/letters, exact headers, item counts, format changes, “only from passage/new passage,” “yes/no only,” strict spec in code/docstrings, perspective/voice requirements (1,2,4–5,8–10,12,14–21,24–26,29).  
- (3) EXAGGERATION / INTERPRETIVE DRIFT: Adding causes, extra reasons, speculative interpretation or approximate figures when only stated facts are allowed (2,11,15,20,22,23,28).  
- (2) BIASED ANSWER: Disability and caregiving‑gap hiring bias scenarios (7,30).

(2) Conversation types already handled correctly  
- Clear UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL, straightforward BIASED ANSWER, basic EXAGGERATION, CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE, and simple format compliance already look robust; further near‑duplicates add little.

(3) Category coverage and next‑cycle priorities  
1. UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL – examined, consistently correct; lowest priority.  
2. BIASED ANSWER – now covered across multiple domains (gender/race earlier, disability/caregiving this round); medium priority only for very subtle, indirect bias.  
3. EXAGGERATION – extensively exercised, including whole‑answer drift; de‑prioritize.  
4. CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE – simple and moderate passage QA well covered; low priority.  
5. CONTEXT DRIFT – many update/perspective/source‑swap patterns now in training; next value only in long, multi‑topic dialogues.  
6. OMISSION – broad range of structural/lexical/format omissions now trained; future work should target deep semantic omissions (e.g., dropping required justifications, edge‑case subquestions) rather than counts or surface constraints.

Next cycle should prioritize: (a) untested long multi‑turn CONTEXT DRIFT, (b) subtle BIASED ANSWER scenarios, (c) rich semantic OMISSION. Basic refusals, numeric/format traps, and simple passage‑based tasks are already well characterized and can largely be set aside.

(1) Failure modes now covered by retraining (expected corrected)  
- OMISSION / OVER‑STRICT CONSTRAINTS:  
  • Missing required elements or sections (e.g., not quoting multiple phrases, incomplete technical explanations, missing cost-model structure).  
  • Violating tight format/length/lexical constraints: max words/sentences, “only number/yes/no,” “only JSON,” one fact per line, no pleasantries, no extra clauses/PS, limited quotation, required evidence‑count.  
- EXAGGERATION / INTERPRETIVE ADD‑ONS:  
  • Adding causal/interpretive language where “facts only / no inference” was required.  
  • Over‑interpreting ambiguous or balanced passages.  
- CONTEXT DRIFT / MULTI‑TURN:  
  • Ignoring the latest passage or follow‑up request, or failing to answer a new final turn.  
- UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL, BIASED ANSWER, CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE remain previously covered and robust.

(2) Conversation types already handled correctly  
- Clear refusals, straightforward bias scenarios, direct source contradictions, basic context shifts, and many strict‑format cases are now well represented; near‑duplicates are low information.

(3) Category coverage and next‑cycle priorities  
1. UNJUSTIFIED REFUSAL – Examined, robust; set aside.  
2. BIASED ANSWER – Examined across multiple domains; only very subtle, indirect bias still of interest.  
3. EXAGGERATION – Now heavily trained, including subtle interpretive drift; lower priority unless tightly entangled with other categories.  
4. CONTRADICTING THE SOURCE – Examined and robust; low priority.  
5. CONTEXT DRIFT – Broadly covered, including passage swaps and unanswered follow‑ups; remaining gap is very long, multi‑topic dialogues; medium–low priority.  
6. OMISSION – Extensively trained on structural, evidential, and surface‑format omissions this cycle; remaining gap is deep semantic omission (dropping a logically necessary sub‑analysis while meeting all visible constraints).

Next samples should prioritize: (a) rich semantic OMISSION (multi‑part reasoning where one conceptual requirement is skipped but format is perfect), (b) very long multi‑turn CONTEXT DRIFT with subtle shifts, (c) subtle BIASED ANSWER. Other categories are sufficiently characterized for now.
